city.name: Sydney
city.description: Central Sydney, a harbour city of sails and sandstone: the Opera House on Bennelong Point, the Harbour Bridge, The Rocks where the colony began, and the ferries of Circular Quay.

tour.title: Sydney Harbour
tour.text: Gadigal Country, where the First Fleet dropped anchor in 1788. Today the harbour is the city's living room: ferries crossing, sails on the water, and a flat white on the quay.

tour.title: Sydney Opera House
tour.text: Jørn Utzon's sails, each shell cut from a single sphere, covered in a million Swedish tiles that wash themselves in the rain. Catch a show, or just sit on the steps at sunset.

tour.title: Sydney Harbour Bridge
tour.text: The Coathanger, opened in 1932: climb the arch 134 m above the water, walk across from The Rocks to Milsons Point, or watch the fireworks pour off it at New Year.

tour.title: Winter among the towers
tour.text: In June the sun stays low over the city and the towers throw long shadows across the streets. The light is gold all day: a good season for the harbour walk from the Quay to the Botanic Garden.

tour.title: Martin Place at lunchtime
tour.text: The city's grand plaza, where Sydney eats its lunch on the steps. On a winter lunchtime {sun:Martin Place|6-21|12:30}% of it is in the sun; in December, {sun:Martin Place|12-21|12:30}%.

tour.title: Hyde Park
tour.text: Avenues of fig trees and the Archibald Fountain, the oldest park in Australia. In winter its sunny lawns shrink from {sun:Hyde Park|6-21|10:00}% at 10:00 to {sun:Hyde Park|6-21|14:00}% by 14:00.

tour.title: Sydney Tower
tour.text: The gold turret at 309 m, the city's tallest since 1981. On a clear day the Blue Mountains show from the observation deck, and the restaurant up top slowly turns the whole city past your table.

tour.title: After dark
tour.text: The city lights up window by window and the bridge glows over the water. Drag to explore, or open Sun access to test a tower of your own.

protection.title: Sydney LEP 2012, clause 6.18
protection.summary: Development may not add to the total shadow on these public places across their protected hours.
protection.source_note: Protected windows as amended by Amendment No 64. The NSW legislation site refused automated access, so they were transcribed from secondary sources; check the official text before relying on them. Places without a verified window show sun now but are not tested.
protection.reading_note: Two readings matter more than any data error. Times: the Standard Time Act 1987 is reported to read times in legal instruments as standard time, which during daylight saving is an hour later on the clock; for Macquarie Place that changes the sun in its window by up to 44 points. Baseline: the clause compares against buildings existing at a fixed date, while this test compares against today's model.
protection.tip: Tip: try the block west of Hyde Park, or just north of Martin Place.

shore.encoding: r: 128 + 2 x signed distance to the shoreline (m, water positive); g: sand; b: rock

seawall.note: Sydney Harbour and Darling Harbour: Hawkesbury sandstone ashlar and its concrete repairs under a sandstone or concrete coping; the tide ranges about 1.8 m.

waves.note: A typical afternoon north-easterly sea breeze over the 4 km reach from Bradleys Head to the bridge; chosen values, not a measurement.

tussock.note: Tussock (trees.json tussock, #315, #326): the native grasses of Barangaroo Reserve's headland (its list, barangaroo.com Botany: Themeda, Poa and Danthonia among its 84 Sydney species; 68,000 grasses were planted), in the Reserve's own planted beds only: OpenStreetMap's natural=scrub inside its outline, not its named lawns, paths and sandstone (Overture base land, OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL; pipeline/grasses.py). Tinted from the shared snow tussock's straw to their green. The parks and the Domain are mown lawn, so none there.

lomandra.note: Lomandra (trees.json lomandra, #326): spiny-headed mat-rush, Lomandra longifolia, the strappy tussock among the Reserve's grasses (6,000 of them in its planting), in the same beds (OpenStreetMap's natural=scrub inside Barangaroo Reserve; pipeline/grasses.py).

trees.note: The mix is the City of Sydney inventory's (trees.survey) species shares by genus: its street trees for mix (gums: brush box, water gum, paperbarks, eucalypts and angophoras 31%, plane trees 25%, deciduous broadleaves 20.5% as elm, evergreen broadleaves 10.7%, figs 5.4%, jacarandas 3.4%, palms 3%, she-oaks 0.9% as casuarina), its park trees for woods.

survey.attribution: City of Sydney, Trees (CC BY 4.0), extracted 2026-11-07: the street and park trees it surveys, with their measured heights

areas.name: First Fleet Park
areas.note: First Fleet Park, between the Museum of Contemporary Art and the wharves: Destination NSW's jacaranda trail names it as the place to see them against the Harbour Bridge and the Opera House (sydney.com, 'Where to see jacarandas in Sydney'). The council's inventory surveys its street trees, not the park's, so the park's mix is the trail's jacarandas with a few figs and palms.

areas.name: Circular Quay West, by the MCA
areas.note: The promenade between the Museum of Contemporary Art and the water: Destination NSW's photographs of the trail show 'jacarandas outside the Museum of Contemporary Art, Circular Quay'. Not in the council's inventory, so its trees take the trail's jacarandas.

areas.name: Wendy Whiteley's Secret Garden
areas.note: Wendy Whiteley's garden on the old railway land above Lavender Bay: Moreton Bay figs, palms and jacarandas, the Harbour Bridge beyond.
